item.title: When is premium economy worth the extra cost?
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
When is premium economy worth the extra cost? We compare five of the world's best-rated airlines Skytrax named these the world's five best premium economy airlines. We examine what sets their cabins apart and whether it's worth paying extra for them. With wider seats, more legroom and upgraded service, premium economy has become one of the most competitive segments of long-haul flying, promising a more comfortable flight without the business class price tag. But the difference between cabins can vary enormously – and some airlines already offer an excellent economy experience. In the 2026 World Airline Awards, based on passenger surveys, Skytrax named EVA Air, Emirates, Singapore Airlines, Cathay Pacific and Virgin Atlantic as the world's five best premium economy airlines. We look at what each offers compared with its own economy cabin – and which upgrades deliver the most noticeable improvements in comfort and service. EVA Air has a strong claim to premium economy expertise: the Taiwanese carrier was the first airline to introduce the cabin, in 1992. It topped Skytrax's 2026 rating and also won the award for best premium economy amenities. The biggest differentiator is space. On EVA's Boeing 777-300ERs, premium economy offers 38in (96.5cm) of seat pitch (the distance between rows of seats), compared with 31-33in (78.7-83.8cm) in economy. Selected Boeing 787-9s go further, with 42in (106.7cm) of pitch, just 28 seats arranged 2-3-2 and a cradle-style recline designed to preserve the space for the passenger behind. For taller travellers, that 42in (106.7cm) pitch is "like having the length of an acoustic guitar before the next seat," says Katy Nastro, travel expert at flight-tracking app Flighty. But EVA's economy cabin is already relatively generous by industry standards. Gary Leff, founder of the frequent flyer site View from the Wing, points out that some of the airline's Boeing 777s still have nine seats across in economy rather than the tighter 10-abreast configuration common elsewhere. Even so, Leff says he would still "far prefer premium economy", thanks to its wider seats, extra legroom and footrests. Nastro adds that "the cost to try premium economy is slightly lower than upgrading fare classes on Emirates or Cathay, where the jump can cost nearly $800 per segment". Worth the upgrade? Particularly appealing for taller travellers on long-haul flights,especially on EVA's newer 787-9s. But its relatively generous economy seats may be sufficient for some. Emirates ranked second in Skytrax's 2026 awards, but took the top spot for both premium economy seats and catering. Its existing premium economy cabin offers a noticeable upgrade from economy, with cream-coloured leather seats, calf and footrests, larger entertainment screens and an upgraded dining service. But whether those extras justify the cost is another matter. Nastro says Emirates' already-strong economy product makes premium economy a harder sell, particularly when the fare can be twice as expensive. While the additional legroom and improved dining are welcome, she questions whether they are enough to justify such a price difference. That could change with the airline's newest premium economy seat. Unveiled in September 2026 for newly delivered Airbus A350s, it features electric controls, wireless charging, a 13.3in (33.8cm) 4K screen and a full-height adjustable privacy divider between each seat, which Emirates says is an industry first for premium economy. The cabin has just 28 seats in a 2-3-2 configuration. The A350 is already operating on routes including Dubai to Kuala Lumpur, but the aircraft type alone does not guarantee the new privacy-divider seat. The airline is introducing the design as it takes delivery of additional aircraft, so passengers hoping to experience it should check with Emirates before booking. Leff is more enthusiastic about the new A350 seat than Emirates' older premium economy product, which he considers "fairly ordinary" by the standards of this group. He says the latest version "could be the best premium economy in the world". Worth the upgrade? The newest A350 seats promise a compelling improvement in privacy and comfort, making them particularly appealing on long-haul flights. The older premium economy cabin is a more modest upgrade: the extra space and better dining are welcome, but whether they're worth paying for depends on the fare difference. Singapore Airlines ranked third for premium economy in 2026, but it also won Skytrax's award for the world's best economy class – making the case for upgrading less straightforward. Premium economy offers roughly 38in (96.5cm) of seat pitch, compared with around 32in (81.3cm) in economy, as well as wider seats, 8in (20.3cm) of recline and built-in calf and footrests. On its A380, its 2-4-2 premium economy configuration also means fewer middle seats than economy's 3-4-3 layout. There are upgrades beyond the seat, too. Passengers can pre-order chef-inspired meals through the airline's Book the Cook service, enjoy Champagne and benefit from priority check in and boarding. Nastro recommends upgrading on overnight journeys and flights lasting more than eight hours. "Sometimes, flights are simply too long to feel comfortable in economy despite the airline offering a solid economy product," says Nastro. She points to the extra legroom and fewer middle seats as particularly valuable on those lengthy routings. Leff, meanwhile, notes that Singapore's economy cabin is already among the more comfortable options for long-haul travellers, with touches such as footrests and cup holders on some aircraft, as well as strong food and entertainment, regardless of cabin. Worth the upgrade? On Singapore Airlines' longest flights, the extra space, recline and leg support could make a difference, particularly overnight. But on shorter journeys, its award-winning economy cabin may be more than comfortable enough. Sometimes, upgrading after booking can be considerably cheaper than buying a premium economy ticket outright. On a recent overnight transatlantic flight, Nastro was offered an upgrade for $238 (€212/£178), much less than the difference between the two fares at the time of booking. "For me, the extra cost was worth it to have a better experience on an overnight flight," she says, particularly because she had to hit the ground running the next day. Cathay Pacific came in fourth overall, while its premium economy seat ranked second only to Emirates' in Skytrax's 2026 awards. On the A350, premium economy offers 40in (101.6cm) of seat pitch, 9in (22.9cm) of recline and full-length leg rests. Passengers also get priority boarding, more baggage and upgraded meals. Meanwhile, Cathay's refurbished Boeing 777-300Ers feature a redesigned premium economy cabin with winged headrests for added privacy, 15.6in (39.6cm) 4K entertainment screens and Bluetooth audio. For Nastro, the newer seat design is what best distinguishes Cathay's premium economy from competitors such as Singapore Airlines. While she finds the benefits of upgrading from economy relatively similar between the two carriers, Cathay's larger entertainment screens make watching films more immersive, and its winged headrests offer a greater sense of privacy. The latter, she says, is the "biggest differentiator". Like Singapore, though, Cathay starts from a strong economy offering, so the main case for upgrading is the seat itself rather than a dramatic change in service. Worth the upgrade? Most persuasive on long overnight flights, when the generous recline and leg support become more valuable. For travellers seeking greater privacy, Cathay's redesigned 777-300ER cabin offers another compelling reason to upgrade, with its winged headrests providing more separation from neighbouring passengers. On shorter journeys, however, the benefits may be less noticeable. Virgin Atlantic rounded out Skytrax's global top five, with a premium economy cabin that combines extra space with a more elaborate onboard experience. Seats offer up to 38in (96.5cm) of pitch, compared with around 31in (78.7cm) in standard economy, along with greater recline and leg support. The amount of personal space varies by aircraft, however. On Virgin's Boeing 787-9s, premium economy seats measure up to 21in (53.3cm) wide and recline 8in (20.3cm), while those on its newer Airbus A350-1000s and A330neos are narrower at 18.5in (47cm) wide. The A330neo also adds wireless charging and Bluetooth-enabled entertainment screens. For Leff, the main attraction of Virgin's premium economy is the extra space, which offers what he describes as a "less claustrophobic experience". Virgin also distinguishes its premium economy cabin through food and service. "There's sparkling wine on boarding, a menu with three main course choices and meals served on china with proper cutlery," says Leff, who adds that afternoon tea can be another nice touch. On the ground, passengers benefit from dedicated check in and bag drop, priority boarding and baggage delivery, plus two checked bags weighing up to 23kg each. Worth the upgrade? Virgin's wider 787 seats may be especially appealing, while the upgraded dining and airport benefits offer additional reasons to pay more. However, travellers primarily interested in legroom may find better value in Virgin's Economy Delight seats, which offer up to 34in (86.4cm) of seat pitch without the full Premium fare. – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: IDEA: These Compression Socks Help Increase Blood Flow and Reduce Swelling at 30,000 Feet
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Frequent fliers understand the importance of a trusty pair of compression socks, especially on a long-haul flight. This simple travel accessory offers a slew of benefits, especially to those who are stationary for hours at a time, like when you're seated on a plane, train, or in a car for a long road trip. These tighter-than-normal socks apply pressure and squeeze the veins in your legs and ankles, which in turn helps improve blood circulation, reduce swelling, and relieve discomfort. If you've ever experienced that awful pins-and-needles feeling after being stuck in the middle seat on a 10+ hour flight, you might want to slip on a pair of compression socks before takeoff. The best compression socks for travel are the right amount of snug, easy to slip on and off, and soft on the skin. Ahead, I've gathered the pairs our editors regularly turn to on long travel days. FAQ: What are the benefits of wearing compression socks? Compression socks can help improve circulation, reduce swelling, and alleviate discomfort or pain in the legs that may result from sitting in the same position for an extended period of time, like on a long flight. By promoting blood flow, compression socks can also help prevent blood clots, including deep vein thrombosis (or DVT), a very rare and dangerous condition in which a blood clot forms in a deep vein in your body and travels to your lungs. Compression socks can also aid in muscle recovery, making them a nice option for athletes too. Who are compression socks best for? Talk to your doctor about your pain points to see if compression socks might be beneficial to you. The right pair can help travelers, as well as pregnant women, athletes, and anyone prone to swelling in the legs or feet. Compression socks can also help relieve swelling and pain caused by varicose veins. What compression level should I look for? To benefit from compression socks, it's important to find a pair that fits well and offers the right millimeters of mercury, or mmHg, for you. The mmHg measurement calculates how much pressure is being exerted. Medical-grade socks sit in the 20-30 mmHg range, while most casual compression socks are still tight enough to encourage circulation at 15-25 mmHg. For reference, socks that are 30 mmHg are extra tight, while pairs that are 10 mmHg are relatively loose. What are graduated compression socks? While shopping for a pair of compression socks, you might notice that some are labeled as graduated compression socks. These pairs apply the greatest amount of pressure at the ankle and gradually decrease in tightness towards the top of the sock, helping blood flow back up towards the heart more effectively. Graduated compression socks are a comfortable choice for travelers who prefer a pair that aren't extremely restrictive all the way through. item.title: Should You Be Tipping in Paris? It Depends!
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Do you tip in Paris? The simple answer: No, tipping is not expected in Paris. While tipping is mandatory in practice in North America (and places like South Africa, Egypt, and Morocco), the act of tipping is not required in France. Because service charges are typically built into the final bill at establishments in France, tipping is seen as a supplementary gesture of appreciation. Don’t believe me, a travel writer and editor who lives in Paris? That’s OK; I’ve only lived here full-time for six months and visited the city a mere 16 times before. Maybe there’s something I don’t yet know! So to get some truly sound advice, I asked for guidance on tipping in France from two of Condé Nast Traveler’s Top Travel Specialists who have expertise in travel to France: Frenchman Mark Bonte of France-based French Side Travel, and Camilla Davidson, Red Savannah’s head of destination management for France, UK, and Ireland. Tipping is not an expected part of the culture in France, certainly not as much as it is in the United States, Davidson explains: “In many instances, there is a sense of pride that pricing is ‘all-inclusive’ and that service is not expected beyond the cost you are charged.” On top of that inclusion of service charges, Bonte explains that hospitality staff in France are salaried employees. “Tips are considered an extra gesture of appreciation rather than part of their expected compensation,” he says. Compare that to the United States, where federal and state labor laws allow employers to pay service workers a lower base wage and rely on customer tips to make up the rest. “That said, tipping at restaurants has become increasingly common, especially for a leisurely lunch or dinner with good service,” Bonte says. “The French approach remains less about calculating a set percentage and more about acknowledging a particularly enjoyable experience or attentive service.” Need more specific situation-based guidance? Read on to learn how much to tip in Paris. This article has been updated since its original publish date. Do you tip at hotels in Paris? Tipping is not mandatory at hotels in Paris, but it is appreciated for personal service. For example, Bonte of French Side Travel says, tipping “two to five euros for a porter or bellhop, or a few euros per day for housekeeping, is a thoughtful gesture, while guests may tip more for exceptional concierge service.” Occasionally, some properties might add a voluntary service charge to your final room bill, but this is typically at your discretion, according to Davidson of Red Savannah. For your edification, she says, you can certainly ask how it is allocated and who will get it. After all, you want to be sure that your appreciation reaches its intended recipient: “If a bartender has made a particularly excellent cocktail or you loved your spa treatment, offering a tip for great service is hugely appreciated—but it’s not an expectation in the same way it would be in the United States.” Do you tip at restaurants in Paris? Even at the best restaurants in Paris, tipping is not required, but it is an expression of thanks for exemplary service. “Service [charge] is already included in the bill, so there is no expectation to add 15 to 20% as in the United States,” says Bonte. But when you tip in Paris, there’s no set-in-stone rule for how much. As a rule of thumb, Bonte says, “If the service was particularly good, leaving a few euros or rounding up the bill is common and always appreciated.” Davidson explains that many restaurants, especially traditional brasseries, will make a point of highlighting that the cost of service is built into the restaurant’s pricing model, with “service compris” written on the bill. Additionally, many waiters in France are professionals and part of official governing bodies for the profession, which means it is illegal for their wages to be made up by gratuities. Do you tip at bars and cafés in Paris? According to Bonte, it is common in cafés to round the tip up to the next whole figure of the total bill. You might leave the change or round up the total; for example, you leave 20 euros on an 18-euro coffee-and-drinks bill. But as is the case for restaurants, there is no obligation to tip at cafés or coffee shops in Paris. This is also a good place to empty your pockets of any loose change you may have (pick up a handy travel wallet when you pack for Paris—the French love their change). Do you tip in taxis and drivers in Paris? For a regular taxi in Paris, simply rounding up the fare is perfectly acceptable. “For a private driver providing a full-day service, however, it is customary to leave a tip,” says Bonte. “Give around 20 to 30 euros per day, depending on the level of service.” That figure could even go up to a generous 50 euros if they offer additional services like acting as a guide. Again, it’s a way to say thanks. For more standard pick-ups and drop-offs, a taxi driver won’t be upset if you simply round up the taxi bill, but it’s by no means essential, says Davidson of Red Savannah. However, if you have a private driver, chauffeur, or guide, Davidson recommends tipping more: “They are enormously appreciative of gratuities, so a 50-euro tip per day would be considered very generous, if you feel it’s representative of the service rendered.” Do you tip in spas in Paris? It is customary and appreciated to leave a tip directly for your therapist after a treatment, especially when the service has been excellent, says Bonte: “Around 10 to 20 euros is generally a nice gesture.” Be sure to check if a service charge has already been included in the final bill, but don’t let that stop you from saying thanks to your therapist through a tip. That’s the basic rule in Paris: A tip is a way to show your gratitude and appreciation for services rendered—no more, no less.

item.title: Here are 10 Full-Sized Liquid Items That You Can Actually Carry On Board a Flight
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
For years, travelers have become accustomed to meticulously packing liquids ranging from shampoo to sunscreen in their carry-on bags in order to meet the TSA liquid limit—and avoid getting that expensive perfume confiscated. Internationally, this rule is known as “3-1-1." Liquids, gels, and creams packed in a carry-on must be in containers no larger than 3.4 ounces (100 mL). All containers must fit in a single, clear, quart-sized bag. (Larger liquids can still be brought along on your travels but must be packed in checked luggage.) While commonly referred to as “liquids,” these regulated substances are technically known as LAGs, an abbreviation for liquids, aerosols, and gels. This category also encompasses creams or pastes—essentially anything that can be cut through or spread with a butter knife—from common travel necessities like shampoo, face wash, and sunscreen, to toothpaste, hairspray, and even peanut butter. The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) first introduced the rule in August 2006, after British police foiled a terrorist plot to detonate explosive liquid in soda cans on flights from London to the US and Canada—prompting countries around the world to adopt the new airport security measure. Today, most countries abide by the rule, though it has loosened in recent years, as more airports install advanced CT scanners with the capability to identify hazardous liquids. Some UK airports, including London Heathrow (LHR), now allow liquids of up to 2 liters (about 67.6 ounces). In the US, a TSA spokesperson tells Condé Nast Traveler they “anticipate the limit on liquids will be lifted in the coming years." However, with the roll-out of the new scanners varying by terminal, the limit still remains in effect nationwide. In this transitional period, the decisions are ultimately up to the individual officers, but it turns out there are certain exceptions to the 3-1-1 rule. The TSA currently allows travelers to take 10 common full-size liquids through airport security in the US. To bring approved oversized liquids through security, travelers need to declare these items to a security officer prior to screening and place them in a separate bin. Anything that triggers the alarm while going through security is subject to further inspection. Here's what you need to know. This story has been updated with new information since its original publication date. Prescription liquids, gels, and aerosols Medication prescribed specifically for you is perhaps the most common item that qualifies as an exception. TSA recommends that it’s clearly labeled so there is no question about what's inside. Depending on the situation, medication may be screened visually or with an X-ray machine and may also be tested for traces of explosives. If security officers are unable to adequately screen an item, you may be asked to open the container for vapor analysis. However, according to the TSA, officers will never place anything inside medically necessary liquids. In cases where you would like to make sure the medication isn’t opened or X-rayed, simply inform the TSA officer. “Additional steps will be taken to clear the liquid, and you or the traveling guardian will undergo additional screening procedures, which may include AIT screening, a pat-down, and screening of your carry-on property,” the site says. Note that prescription wet pet food does not count as an exception and must abide by the 3-1-1 rule and must abide by the 3-1-1 rule, even for service animals. Liquid medications and contact lens solution In general, liquid medications that are not prescriptions are limited to 3.4 ounces, but TSA does allow “larger amounts of medically necessary liquids, gels, and aerosols in reasonable quantities for your trip"—such as inhalers, insulin (which should be placed in a separate bin for X-ray screening), and nebulizer liquid—with the caveat you must declare them to security officers first. It's also advised that all medications are labeled to further ensure the security process goes smoothly. Contact lens solution also falls into this category. However, the agency notes that “some contact lens solutions contain chemicals that typically alarm and may not permitted through the checkpoint,” and therefore recommends packing contact lens solutions over 3.4 ounces in your checked baggage. Ice packs, including frozen water bottles If you're somebody who likes to bring your own cooler filled with food on the plane, know that gel ice and freezer packs are permitted. This includes frozen water bottles, as long as they are frozen solid when they pass through, and liquid-filled teethers—a helpful note for parents with young children. However, any portion that has been partially melted and slushy, or any liquid at the bottom of the container, will count toward the 3-1-1 limit. The only exception is medically-necessary gel ice packs—for items such as breast milk, IV bags, pumps, and syringes—which are allowed in “reasonable qualities,” even if they are melted or slushy. Traveling with infants is challenging enough already. It's a good thing, then, that breast milk and baby formula are categorized as “medically necessary liquids" permitted by the TSA. (The child does not need to be present for this exception.) The TSA suggests—but doesn't require—that the liquids be transported in clear and translucent bottles, so they can be screened by the Bottle Liquid Scanners (those in pouches may not be able to). While there is a chance you may be asked to open them, nothing will ever be placed in the liquid. The agency also adds that the screening process shouldn't affect the formula, but if you prefer they not be X-rayed, alternative testing means can be requested. While baby powder is not a liquid, note that powder-like substances that are more than 12 ounces do need to be placed in a separate bin for screening. However, if you can, TSA suggests putting them in checked baggage. In addition to breast milk and formula, food and drinks for babies and toddlers are allowed, including juices and puree pouches since they technically fall into the “medically necessary” category. Water for babies is also allowed in “reasonable quantities," but needs to be removed and screened separately from other belongings. There are some portable electronic devices which require non-spillable batteries with absorbed electrolyte, like a gel cell, absorbed glass mat, and the like. As long as the equipment is protected against accidental activation or evolution of heat, and the battery's voltage is 12 volts or less with less than 100 watt hours, then it makes it cut. But no more than two spare batteries can be carried. Yes, you can put all your eggs in one basket—or your one carry-on bag without abiding by 3-1-1 rules. Even liquid yolks can be taken through security but may need to be removed from the carry-on bag for proper inspection, to make sure the X-ray machines show they’re truly what they're cracked up to be. It's suggested to pack them separately and keep them “uncluttered” ahead of time to ensure a quick screening. Assuming your live fish and live coral in water need more than 3.4 ounces of water to survive, they can be taken in your carry-on—but not in checked bags. They do need to be in a clear transparent container and properly inspected by the TSA officer. Certain airlines also permit live lobster, but the agency suggests checking your carrier's website ahead of time to avoid being caught in a pinch. Liquid exceptions can be made in the name of science. Non-infectious specimens in preservative solution, which can include formaldehyde, ethanol, isopropanol, or other alcohols, can be carried through if they're for scientific research—but they’ll need to be packed quite specifically. There can be up to 30 milliliters of free liquid in a heat-sealed inner plastic bag and no more than one liter in the entire outer packaging, which needs to be marked: "Scientific research specimens, 49 CFR 173.4b applies." Specific instructions can be found here. Duty-free items in officially sealed bags on inbound international flights Plenty of airports lead you through a massive duty-free shop before the departure gate, tempting you with local products and international brands. Whether they're Canadian maple syrup, French wine, or South African sauces, liquid souvenirs can be taken home so long as they are properly sealed by the retailer in a security tamper-evident bag (STEB) and show no signs of being tampered with. The purchase must've been made within 48 hours—and make sure to hold onto your original receipt as necessary proof. The global system was developed in 2008 “to allow an exemption" to liquid volume rules for items purchased at duty-free airport retailers or on board an aircraft, according to the International Civil Aviation Organization. For US travelers, this is limited to inbound international flights, according to the TSA. Note that not every airport shop offers the STEB option.

item.title: United Airlines baggage fees and how to avoid paying them
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
United Airlines baggage fees and how to avoid paying them Checked baggage fees and carry-on allowances vary depending on your United Airlines ticket. While many travelers must pay to check a bag, others qualify for one or more free checked bags. Your baggage allowance depends on several factors, including your destination, fare type, elite status and whether you hold an eligible United cobranded credit card. Here's everything you need to know about United Airlines' baggage fees and policies. United Airlines allows all passengers to bring one personal item on board for free. Personal items must fit under the seat in front of you and measure no more than 9 inches by 17 inches by 10 inches. Examples include backpacks, purses, briefcases, laptop bags and approved pet carriers. Most passengers can also bring one full-size carry-on bag at no additional cost. Carry-on bags must measure no more than 22 inches by 14 inches by 9 inches, including handles and wheels. However, passengers traveling on United basic economy tickets are generally limited to only a personal item. Those who bring a full-size carry-on bag to the gate must check it and pay the applicable checked baggage fee, plus a $25 gate handling charge. There are several exceptions to this basic economy restriction, including: - Flights to Canada, South America and across the Atlantic, as well as international flights across the Pacific - MileagePlus Premier members and eligible companions traveling on the same reservation - Primary cardholders of eligible United MileagePlus credit cards Passengers whose carry-on bags exceed United's size limits may also be required to check them and pay any applicable baggage fees. United Airlines' checked baggage fees vary based on your destination, fare type, bag weight and size, elite status and whether you hold an eligible United credit card. To determine how much you'll pay for your specific itinerary, use the baggage fee calculator on United's website. United Airlines baggage fees within North America, Central America and the Caribbean United Airlines' checked bag fees for flights within North America, Central America and the Caribbean are pretty straightforward. And, in most cases, if you prepay for your bags at least 24 hours before departure, you'll receive $5 off each of the first two checked bags. These fees apply to standard economy tickets without complimentary baggage benefits and may vary by route and ticket purchase date. The standard checked baggage weight limit is 50 pounds per bag for economy passengers without elite status. MileagePlus Premier members and passengers traveling in business or first class generally have a 70-pound allowance per bag. United Airlines baggage fees for long-haul international destinations United Airlines' checked baggage fees for long-haul international flights vary by destination and fare type. Here's what economy passengers can generally expect: - South America: Most standard economy tickets include one free checked bag, while a second bag generally costs $100. Basic economy passengers may pay around $90 for their first bag and $100 for their second. - Europe: Standard economy passengers generally receive one free checked bag, with a $120 fee for a second bag. Basic economy passengers typically pay $90 for their first bag and $120 for their second. - Asia: Standard economy passengers generally receive two free checked bags. Basic economy allowances vary by destination, with some routes including a free first checked bag and others charging a fee. - Africa and Australia: Standard economy passengers generally receive one free checked bag, with a potential $100 fee for a second. Basic economy allowances vary by destination. These fees are subject to change and may differ based on your route, ticket purchase date and MileagePlus status. Again, it's helpful to check United's baggage fee calculator for your specific itinerary. United Airlines' standard checked baggage weight limit is 50 pounds for economy and premium economy passengers, including those with Star Alliance Gold status or eligible United credit cards. MileagePlus Premier members and passengers traveling in business or first class can generally check bags weighing up to 70 pounds without incurring overweight fees. For bags exceeding the applicable weight or size limits, additional fees may apply: - Overweight bags: Fees generally range from $100 to $300 for bags weighing 51 to 70 pounds and $200 to $500 for bags weighing 71 to 100 pounds, depending on the route. - Oversized bags: Fees generally start at $200 for bags measuring more than 62 linear inches (length plus width plus height), including handles and wheels. United generally doesn't accept checked bags weighing more than 100 pounds, though exceptions apply to certain special items. Overweight and oversized fees may apply in addition to standard checked baggage fees. United Airlines generally charges $200 for a third checked bag on domestic U.S. flights. Fees for additional bags vary by destination. United accepts excess baggage on a space-available basis, and certain destinations and routes may have additional restrictions, including seasonal limits on the number of bags passengers can check. Skis, snowboards, hang gliding equipment, parachutes and many more items can count as a checked bag on United Airlines (or sometimes as a carry-on, depending on the item) as long as they meet the requirements. In most cases, there are no additional fees beyond any applicable checked-bag or overweight fees (except for on scuba tanks). Also, United will not accept kayaks or canoes. You can check out the requirements and fees for checking sports equipment on United's website. How to avoid United Airlines baggage fees Luckily, there are several ways to avoid paying United Airlines baggage fees if you plan to check baggage on your next flight. All status levels in United's MileagePlus program offer checked bag benefits for those flying within the U.S. and between the U.S., Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. All bags can weigh up to 70 pounds. - Premier Silver members receive a free first checked bag for themselves and up to nine traveling companions on the same reservation. - Premier Gold members can check up to two bags for free for themselves and up to nine traveling companions on the same reservation. - Premier Platinum, Premier 1K and Global Services members can generally check three bags for themselves and up to nine traveling companions on the same reservation, subject to destination-specific restrictions. Additionally, Star Alliance Gold members receive at least one free first checked bag on all United-operated flights. First standard checked bag free: First and second standard checked bags free: The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Passengers traveling in United Polaris business class (not on a basic business fare), United Business or United First generally receive two free checked bags weighing up to 70 pounds each. United Premium Plus passengers also receive two free checked bags, though the standard weight limit is 50 pounds per bag unless they qualify for a higher allowance through MileagePlus Premier status. Several travel rewards cards offer annual statement credits that can help offset checked baggage fees. For example, the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) offers a $300 annual travel credit that can be used toward eligible travel purchases, including airline baggage fees. Meanwhile, American Express Platinum Card® offers up to $200 in annual airline fee credits for eligible incidental charges, including checked baggage fees. Enrollment is required, and you must select United Airlines as your qualifying airline to receive statement credits for eligible baggage charges. There are many moving parts to United Airlines' baggage policy, but there are many ways for passengers to avoid checked baggage fees. When in doubt, the baggage fee calculator on United's website is your best friend. If you log in to the United website, you can even search for your specific itinerary and get the most up-to-date information on United baggage fees.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Virgin Atlantic Flying Club: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Virgin Atlantic Flying Club: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more Despite switching to dynamic pricing in 2024, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club continues to offer noteworthy Saver-level fares and attractive partner award charts. Though booking through this U.K.-based carrier loyalty program can sometimes be costly when factoring in taxes and fees and additional surcharges on award tickets, some sweet spots remain. Plus, since Flying Club partners with major credit card rewards programs with regular transfer bonuses, points and miles enthusiasts can easily book and take advantage of these promotions. item.title: 'Royal Jewellery: From Coronations to Keepsakes': More than 300 royal jewels to go on display at Buckingham Palace in new exhibition
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
From glittering coronation diamonds to intimate family keepsakes, more than 300 royal jewels will be displayed at Buckingham Palace in summer 2027, many of which have never been seen by the public before. Opening on 25 June 2027, Royal Jewellery: From Coronations to Keepsakes will be the first exhibition to explore 500 years of British royal jewellery, with around two-thirds of the pieces going on public display for the very first time. Hosted at The King’s Gallery, Buckingham Palace, the exhibition will feature jewellery worn by monarchs from Henry VIII to Queen Elizabeth II, alongside paintings, designs and historical documents from the Royal Collection and Royal Archives. Among the highlights will be the Diamond Diadem, which visitors might recognise from portraits of Queen Elizabeth II, who wore it in images reproduced on everything from postage stamps to banknotes. The dazzling piece actually dates back to George IV, for whose coronation it was originally commissioned. Visitors will also be able to admire Queen Victoria's Small Diamond Crown, which became so closely associated with the monarch that it was placed on her coffin during her lying in state. While the Crown Jewels will remain at the Tower of London, the exhibition will feature designs by some of the world's most prestigious jewellery houses, including Cartier, Boucheron, Fabergé and Garrard & Co. Perhaps the most touching objects, however, are those belonging to Queen Victoria. Among them is a rather unusual brooch containing her eldest daughter's first milk tooth, which Prince Albert removed himself. Other keepsakes offer a glimpse into the couple's relationship, from a diamond brooch Albert presented to Victoria before their wedding to a mourning ring containing his photograph and their intertwined cyphers. There will be plenty of pieces that even devoted royal watchers may never have seen, including a serpent-shaped bracelet belonging to Queen Alexandra and a Fabergé pendant, decorated with aquamarine and diamonds, that Queen Mary gave to her granddaughter, the future Elizabeth II. Queen Charlotte's garnet jewels and the Greville emerald and diamond necklace, part of Dame Margaret Greville's bequest to Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother, will also be displayed publicly for the first time. Not all the stories are romantic, however. Visitors will also encounter objects connected to the execution of Charles I, including cufflinks said to have been worn by the monarch on the scaffold, later passed to his loyal supporters. "This unprecedented exhibition will bring together some of the most important and spectacular royal jewels in British history, many never exhibited publicly before," said co-curators Caroline de Guitaut and Kathryn Jones. The exhibition will run for nine months, until 19 March 2028, and will be accompanied by a book of the same name, described as the first comprehensive study of the British royal jewellery collection. When can you book tickets? Tickets for Royal Jewellery: From Coronations to Keepsakes will go on sale to Royal Collection Trust e-newsletter subscribers on Wednesday 28 October 2026, with general bookings opening on Tuesday 3 November via rct.uk. To qualify for early access, visitors must subscribe to the newsletter by the end of Tuesday 27 October. The exhibition will run from 25 June 2027 to 19 March 2028 at The King’s Gallery, Buckingham Palace, London.

item.title: IDEA: The 10 best things to do in London this weekend

When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (16 - 18 October) Pulitzer Prize-winning opera Angel's Bone arrives at the London Coliseum following its UK premiere at Manchester’s Aviva Studio in spring. The run is part of the English National Opera's dual-centre model, bringing opera to audiences in both Greater Manchester and London – with productions shaped by the venues in which they’re performed. Angel’s Bone tells the story of Mr and Mrs X.E., a desperate couple longing for a better life who discover two wounded angels in their garden. However, what begins as an act of compassion takes a darker turn, highlighting human greed and socially relevant issues. Address: London Coliseum, St Martin's Lane, London WC2N 4ES Argentine bakery Madre is the latest business to take residency in King’s Cross – and the treats are well worth making time for. The coffee shop at Fabrica X is part of The Mills Fabrica, a platform that supports innovation across techstyle and agrifood, with a focus on sustainability and social impact. Think small-batch, indulgent bites that pair fabulously well with their usual coffee offering. Address: The Mills Fabrica, 36-40 York Way, London N1 9AB A handful of new drinking dens have opened across the capital recently, just in time for cosy autumn evenings spent nursing a pint (or stronger concoction, should you so choose). The Last Exchange is the city’s newest pub, having opened its doors in Exchange Square, a stone’s throw from Liverpool Street Station. The team is determined to ‘pub properly’, with all the tipples you can imagine and a menu of elevated classics. Sip on a pint of The City Scribbler, the pub’s own house beer, and feel the stresses of city life fizzle away. Elsewhere, Bar Buah has started welcoming thirsty foodies at The White Horse, Peckham. Ex-Oranj chef Elies Salvà Ruiz de Villegas is in charge, so expect dishes such as crab caldereta and oxtail croquetas to go down very well with a glass of wine. Address: The Last Exchange, 11 Exchange Square, Broadgate, London EC2A 2BR; Bar Buah at The White Horse Peckham Website: publicanestate.com; whitehorsepeckham.co.uk 4. Cackle away as he explores the wonders and the weaknesses of human memory, touching on the nights he’ll never forget along the way. Address: Leicester Square Theatre, 6 Leicester Place, London WC2H 7BX BREW//LDN goes Bavarian for its first-ever Oktoberfest celebration this weekend, uniting 18 breweries in the same space for two days of beer-sloshing. More than 35 beers are available on tap at the site, found at Riverside East in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, plus a live oompah band, DJs and street food stalls. Address: Riverside East, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, 5 Thornton St, London E20 2AD 6. Pick up affordable pieces in Battersea Aesthetes and art lovers come together under one roof as the Affordable Art Fair Battersea returns for its autumn edition this week. The fair offers an accessible introduction to collecting with thousands of works priced under £10,000 across multiple spaces – with more than 100 galleries participating. Address: Battersea Evolution, Battersea Park, Queenstown Road, London SW11 4NJ Celebrate six years of Michelin-starred Kol, recognised as one of the best restaurants in the world, as the team throw a one-night-only celebration this Sunday. Chef and founder Santiago Lastra is transforming the restaurant into a dynamic culinary festival as four of the city’s most celebrated chefs, including Margo Henderson and Jeremy Lee, interpret iconic Mexican dishes in their own way. Tickets cost £135 per person and include a glass of biodynamic wine Gut Oggau, five dishes, and a cocktail. Address: KOL, 9 Seymour Street, London W1H 7BA 8. Address: Art Café By Thibault Hauchard, Brook's Mews, London W1K 4HR 9. Savour a range of limited-edition cocktails as performers including Madeleine (13 October) and Kianja (21 October) bring the soul above the colourful chaos of Soho. item.title: Where was 'Hocus Pocus' filmed? Inside the real-life Salem locations that the Sanderson sisters haunt
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Hocus Pocus filmed? Salem will forever be synonymous with witches. Between February 1692 and May 1693, 20 people were found guilty of witchcraft, with more than 200 accused. So it’s no surprise then that Disney’s most famous Halloween film, 1993’s Hocus Pocus, was set here. It follows a teenage boy, Max, who accidentally brings three 17th-century witches – the Sanderson sisters – back to life (played by Bette Midler, Sarah Jessica Parker and Kathy Najimy) one Halloween. The three sisters must make a potion using the soul of a young child to stay alive, with Max, his younger sister Dani, his love interest Allison and a cursed cat named Thackery Binx all banding together to try to stop them. Of course, much of the filming took place in Salem, so you can actually retrace the Sanderson sisters’ footsteps – if you dare… Where was Hocus Pocus filmed? The opening scenes of the film are among the most memorable, as a human Thackery Binx discovers that his sister Emily has been lured into their creepy house by the Sanderson sisters. Set in the 1600s in Salem, it needed a suitably Puritan aesthetic, so the production turned to Pioneer Village, a living museum in the town’s Forest River Park. Built in 1930, it sits on three acres of land and contains a few examples of different colonial architecture, including the thatched-roof cottages used in Hocus Pocus. Max and Allison’s high school, John Bailey High, features throughout the film, first at the beginning and later on when they lure the witches to the on-site furnace in the hopes of killing them. The cookie-cutter school building was a real school – Phillips Elementary – which had rather conveniently closed down in 1992. After filming, it was turned into private residential housing, so sadly you can’t still see it. Max and Dani’s new home in Salem feels particularly typical of New England architecture. Not only was it built in the 1800s, but it boasts wooden siding, a porch, and a distinctive lookout tower in the attic bedroom belonging to Max – a feature which becomes a major plot point later in the film when the witches take Dani from here. It’s still a private home and was sold a few years ago for just under £655K. It’s during Trick-or-Treating that we first see Allison’s palatial home, an impressive white-fronted building that prompts Max and Dani to remark that it must belong to rich people. The house used as a stand-in is owned by the Peabody Essex Museum, and is known for being one of the best examples of an 18th-century mansion in Salem. It’s thought to have been built in the 1720s, in the Georgian Colonial style, with ionic columns flanking the entrance. At the beginning of the film, when Max is struggling to fit in at his new school, he is accosted by local bullies, Jay and Ernie, in the local cemetery. These scenes, in which they steal his trainers and leave him to cycle home in just socks, were filmed at Old Burial Mill in the nearby town of Marblehead. The cemetery is one of the oldest burial grounds in New England and contains the graves of several Salem Witch Trial victims. The nighttime cemetery scenes featuring Billy the zombie were filmed indoors on a sound stage in California. The famous party scene in the film, where Bette Midler’s character sings I Put A Spell On You and bewitches the town’s adult population, was shot in the ballroom at the Park Plaza Hotel in Los Angeles. The hotel was built in 1925 by architect Claud Beelman, who went on to become a prominent member of the Art Deco movement, and is designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 267. It’s been used as a filming location for countless other music videos, TV shows and films, including 2013’s Gangster Squad starring Ryan Gosling and Emma Stone and Guns N' Roses' " Welcome to the Jungle.

item.title: United adds Bermuda flight, bolsters San Francisco hub in 4-route expansion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
United adds Bermuda flight, bolsters San Francisco hub in 4-route expansion United Airlines already revealed its big international "route drop" for next summer. But this weekend, the carrier also revealed a handful of new, shorter routes that will launch in 2027. United is adding a new nonstop flight to Bermuda for the summer season. Plus, the carrier is bolstering its San Francisco International Airport (SFO) hub with a trio of new and returning routes. There's new transcontinental service to New England and the South Carolina coast — and a flight to Oklahoma that the airline hasn't flown since the pandemic. All told, it's a four-route expansion for the Chicago-based carrier, which will cover a total of six cities. The news was first reported by Ishrion Aviation. United will use Boeing 737 family aircraft for three of the four routes, including its Chicago service to Bermuda and its two new transcontinental flights from San Francisco. Its SFO flights to Oklahoma City will be on board an Embraer 175 regional jet. United's new O'Hare service to Bermuda will give the carrier a second nonstop flight to the British overseas territory, which is located about 650 miles off the North Carolina coast. United already offers Bermuda service from its hub at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). Meanwhile, two of the San Francisco routes the carrier is adding will be familiar to longtime United flyers in certain pockets of the country. The carrier last operated its SFO-BDL flights in 2018. Its SFO-OKC service ended in April 2020, during the early days of the pandemic. The Charleston flight, meanwhile, will give Bay Area travelers a new way to explore a popular vacation spot in South Carolina. This latest four-route expansion for United comes a week after the carrier announced a handful of new Canada routes, as part of a larger strengthening of its ties with Air Canada. item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to spend 3 days in Dublin: Michelin seafood, historic pints and stunning cliff hikes
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Dublin’s compact size makes it infinitely explorable in three days, with plenty of time to take in the city centre sights, as well as those a tram ride away. History and literature will obviously be high on the list, brought to life by innovative museums and enthusiastic guides; but Irish culture is also driven by music and community, so knowing the best pub for a pint is crucial, as is knowing the best tables to book on the vibrant restaurant scene. Although many visitors might not realise, the Irish capital’s coast is also easily accessible via the Dart train that runs along the bay; that means cliffside hikes, wildlife-spotting, even sea swimming and sauna-ing all within a hop from town. I love suggesting a seaside jaunt for anyone looking to experience a more local side of the city, to stretch the legs and breathe in the salt-tinged air. Here’s how to make the most of 3 days in Dublin Start your day with a sticky cherry bun and coffee from Bewley’s on Grafton Street, whose original 1920s mosaic-style shopfront was inspired by the Egyptomania that gripped the world after the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb. Stroll down Grafton Street to Trinity College – Ireland’s oldest university, dating from 1592 – and explore the cobblestoned campus on a Trinity Trails tour with a student or alumni guide (past pupils range from Bram Stoker to Paul Mescal, although sadly it’s doubtful he’ll be leading the tour). Follow it with a visit to the university’s spectacular Old Library and the technicolour Book of Kells experience, which projects a ninth-century sacred manuscript on the walls in vivid 3D. Next up is a more quirky take on history at the Little Museum of Dublin on St Stephen’s Green, where part-storyteller, part-stand-up comedian guides will regale you with tales of the city on a 29-minute tour. You’ll need those extra few minutes because your lunch spot will invariably have a queue: Morso on Drury Street serves up generous fillings such as chicken parm and roast beef on its homemade schiacciata Tuscan bread. Stick it out – it’s worth the wait. Walk through Temple Bar and over the Ha’penny Bridge to get the tram to Kilmainham Gaol. This former prison, built in 1796, once held many of Ireland’s most famous revolutionaries. Be sure to book online here beforehand for hour-long guided tours that take in the sky-lit Victorian East Wing and the chapel where 1916 republican leader Joseph Plunkett wed his sweetheart Grace Clifford before being executed a few hours later. You might have time for a pre-dinner pint in the home of Ireland’s most famous stout, the Guinness Storehouse – about 15 minutes away. Or if whiskey is more your thing, Roe & Co distillery is also nearby for a snifter in its Powerhouse bar. Variety Jones has a Michelin star but the vibe in the bare-brick space, furnished with colourful art and chairs, is laidback. The globetrotting six-course chef’s choice menu might include pork and prawn dumping, spaghetti alfredo and barbecued halibut with mussels, kicked off with an aperitif of vermouth made from hedgerow botanicals in County Kerry. Finish the night with music in Arthur’s Jazz Club nearby. If you’re in need of a hearty start to the day, grab a breakfast roll (basically a fry-up in bread and a much-loved Irish classic) in locals’ haunt Declan and Donal’s deli, then head just down the road to 14 Henrietta Street. At this excellent museum, the guides bring the patina-ed walls to life, tracing 300 years of social history in one Georgian house – from its beginnings as the grand home of a viscount to becoming a tenement where 100 people lived. Afterwards, take the Luas tram from Parnell Square to Glasnevin Cemetery, where many notable Irish figures, such as the revolutionary Michael Collins and the suffragist Constance Markievicz, are buried. Climb the 198 steps to the top of Ireland’s highest round tower for views of the city edged by sea and mountains. Your lunch spot is just over the cemetery wall in John Kavanagh’s, known as the Gravediggers after the men who used to drink here after their strenuous night shift. Order a pint of Guinness and a plate of beef stew, and soak up the old-school atmosphere of the timeworn pub, which had been run by the same family since 1833. Grab a cab back into town for a late-afternoon browse around the city’s so-called creative quarter, with Drury Street at the heart of it. Here you’ll find Ireland’s oldest vintage shop, Jenny Vander, selling costume jewellery from the 1920s and frothy Fifties ballgowns, as well as the contemporary crafts of the Irish Design Shop, including heavenly table linen by Jennifer Slattery (her own shop across the River Liffey in Smithfield is also worth a visit). The entrance to the handsome Victorian redbrick George’s Street Arcade is here too; walk a loop, passing record stores and fabric stalls, then take in another grand shopping hub, the Powerscourt Centre, where the entrance is scented by the wild bouquets of floral studio The Garden. Literature lovers should make a beeline for Ulysses Rare Books on the other side of Grafton Street. Pop over to The Long Haul pub, where the original Victorian interior gleams gold and red, for a drink before dinner at Uno Mas. This stalwart of Dublin's casual dining scene serves up Spanish-inspired dishes that hit the spot after a day exploring the city: gooey tortilla, beef tartare, lobster rice, Manchego agnolotti. The space is always buzzy, and wine comes by the glass or the carafe if you don’t want to commit to a bottle. Today is a day for the seaside. It’s easy to forget that Dublin is a coastal capital, and you can’t go wrong venturing north or south to its villagey neighbourhoods via the Dart railway line. But first: breakfast. Grab pastries and coffee from popular bakery Bread 41 on Pearse Street before strolling to the nearby station and heading north to Howth. Book a coastal hike that sets off from the harbourside village to explore woodland, heath, cliffs and beaches while learning about local history. You’ll have worked up an appetite for a late seafood lunch at Mamó – nab a spot at the counter on the ground floor for a more casual take on the elevated cooking that got this place listed in the Michelin Guide. Get the Dart back into town, hopping off at Connolly Station to walk to the Irish Emigration Museum, where immersive galleries and interactive displays tell the story of the millions-strong Irish diaspora worldwide. As JFK (who himself had Irish roots) said: “Most countries send out oil or iron, steel or gold, some other crops, but Ireland has had only one export and that's been people.” Afterwards, walk along the river to explore The Jeanie Johnston, a replica of a 19th-century ship that would have carried thousands of emigrants across the Atlantic to their new homeland. Perhaps JFK failed to mention that Ireland’s other greatest export to the world was its literature. Witness this rich creative heritage at the Abbey, Ireland’s national theatre, where the playbill could include the short stories of podcaster BlindBoy or a premiere from a new Irish playwright. (And if you don’t make an evening performance, you can go on a behind-the-scenes tour most mornings, learning about the history of this legendary theatre). Check out the Abbey’s website for the latest shows. It feels fitting to end your Dublin trip with some music; McNeill’s pub, about a 10-minute walk away, has live performances seven days a week.

item.title: REVIEW: My Favorite Airbnb: A Restored 200-Year-Old Trullo in Puglia With Room for My Whole Family
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
As anyone who has ever planned a family vacation knows, booking a home that satisfies all of your party’s needs is a true art. By the time my parents, brother, and I embarked upon six days in Puglia in September, I had spent hours searching for a home that checked all the boxes. The nonnegotiables: My dad was set on staying in a trullo (the historic, conical stone homes native to the Itria Valley), my mother wanted laundry, and we all wanted a pool. And for me, a former design editor, aesthetics were always critical. These criteria triangulated to find us at Trullo Giulio, 15 minutes outside of Martina Franca. Our host coordinated with her neighbor, Anna, to meet us at the property after the 90-minute drive from Bari. We could hear Anna’s tiny red farm truck puttering down the road to greet us, which should give you an image of just how rural this part of the region is—nothing but olive trees as far as the eye can see. Between my father’s three years of Italian lessons and some universal sign language, we got the lay of the land, which consisted of the main trullo (two beds, one bath) and two outbuildings that hosted two additional bedrooms, a bathroom, and the kitchen. The decor was almost Santorinian in its whitewashed and blue-accented simplicity. The owners had taken great care to decorate the trullo with local textiles and pottery (I highly recommend a day trip to Grottaglie, the ceramic destination of the region) and features that allowed the original stone walls and vaulted ceilings to breathe. It’s modernized, but still retains its charm. And yes, there were a few quirks. The bedrooms in the main trullo were curtained off from the living room—don’t worry, the bathroom had a door—and the advertised AC units were only in the outbuildings. The Wi-Fi and cell service were pretty much nonexistent, which all but highlighted the fact that the true heart of the home was really the outdoor space. The first thing we did after our tour with Anna was take in the pool. As the sun was setting, we dunked our tired feet in the water while sipping the local rosé and snacks Anna had left for us. Saltwater, with a whirlpool and an infinity edge that lets you gaze straight into the olive groves—it’s the showstopper of the property hands down. There’s also an outdoor shower for a quick rinse and multiple lounging spaces both in and out of the sun. We spent the majority of our time—when we weren’t on the pool deck—at the massive dining table under a shaded pergola. While we easily could have spent all of our days lounging poolside, the location of the trullo also made it a convenient launchpad for exploring the region. Aside from the much-slept-on town of Martina Franca, it's within an hour's drive of Alberobello, Ostuni, Polignano a Mare, and the many smaller beach towns along the coast—don’t miss the restaurant Ricciolandia if you’re a fan of urchin. Within a five-minute drive of the house is a delightfully well-stocked mini market and local fave Sale e Pepe, where we had more than one night of phenomenal pizza and grilled meats. My favorite meal in Puglia, however, was one of (mostly) our own making. The final nonnegotiable we’d all agreed upon was that we had to take a pasta-making class before leaving Italy, which we also found on Airbnb. We joined Cristiana and her mother at their beachside trullo in Cozze for a sunny afternoon spent in the outdoor kitchen, where the humbling experience of making orecchiette by hand was enhanced by homemade limoncello and sparkling conversation. No number of ancient churches, fun beach spots, or magical little towns could outweigh the best part of a family trip: The moments spent around the table. Trullo Giulio was the home base we needed to make those moments happen.

item.title: IDEA: The 6 best Alaska cruise shore excursions — from heli-hiking to whale watching
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The 6 best Alaska cruise shore excursions — from heli-hiking to whale watching There are some cruise destinations — Barcelona or Sydney, for instance — where you really don't need to sign up for shore excursions. You can just walk off the ship and head to the major attractions on your own. For the most part, the ports of Alaska aren't like that. To get the most out of an Alaska cruise, you'll want to sign up for a tour in most, if not all, of the ports you visit. And not just any old tour. You'll want the best Alaska shore excursions that get you out into the Alaska backcountry. In Alaska, many of the biggest "attractions" — breathtaking mountain landscapes, glaciers, fjords, breaching whales and feeding bears, for instance — are related to the great outdoors. As a result, many of the best Alaska shore excursions for cruisers are found outside of the towns where ships stop. If you just stay in the towns and explore on your own, you'll miss a big part of what Alaska is all about. Picking the best Alaska shore excursions People who know me know that I love talking about what to do in Alaska ports. This isn't just because I've spent nearly three decades writing about cruising to Alaska and other destinations for major newspapers and magazines. For many years, I also was the co-author of Frommer's "Alaska Cruises & Ports of Call" guide. In researching nearly half a dozen editions of that book, I spent many days exploring each of the major cruise ports in the state. I've tried a large number of the shore excursions in places such as Juneau, Skagway and Ketchikan. And I've also poked around these towns a lot on my own. As noted above, my biggest message to anyone planning an Alaska cruise is: get out of the towns. Sign up for something — a hike, a rafting trip, a train ride, a fishing outing — that gets you into Alaska's spectacular outdoor settings. But I also have a few specific, top-line pro tips when you're thinking about the best Alaska shore excursions: - Get up in the air. It will be expensive. We're talking $250 or more per person. But there's nothing quite like seeing the grandeur of Alaska from a helicopter or floatplane. The Juneau Icefield, in particular, is a sight to behold. It covers around 1,500 square miles, an enormous area. You can see it on a flightseeing tour from Juneau, with some tours including landings on the ice. - Don't miss the whales. Even if you're not a big wildlife person, you'll be mesmerized by the humpback whales of Alaska. They are huge (at up to 52 feet in length, longer than a Greyhound bus), and there are boat tours that will get you up close to them. The best places to do this are out of Juneau and Icy Strait Point, if your ship stops there. - Splurge for a trip to Misty Fjords National Monument. This glacier-carved wilderness area, not far from Ketchikan, is another can't-miss sight. It's everything you think of when you think of Alaska: icy blue lakes, waterfalls, snowcapped peaks and glacial valleys. The only way to get there is on a boat or floatplane tour, and they typically start at over $200 a person. Unfortunately, as you can see from the above, many of the most spectacular excursions in Alaskan ports are expensive. But Alaska is not a place to skimp. Alaska is a destination where you may want to budget almost as much per person for your shore excursions as you do for your cabin. That said, you don't have to splurge for a big outing at every call. In Juneau, for instance, you can get an outdoor experience with a relatively inexpensive trip to nearby Mendenhall Glacier. It's just 13 miles from the cruise ship docks and reachable by shuttle bus or taxi. The shuttle buses that go there (there are two companies offering such service, Juneau Tours and M&M Tours) will set you back $65 to $79 per person round-trip, which I find an unconscionable gouge. If you have a few people, you're better off with a taxi, which runs around $40 to $50 each way. For two or three people traveling together, it's not all that pricey a trip. Either way you do it, you'll find some nice hiking trails around Mendenhall Glacier and a visitor center. There's a creek there, too, where I've sometimes seen salmon running. One time, I even saw a bear. Speaking of which: A bear is something you think you want to see in Alaska until you actually see one. Then, you're just hoping you don't get eaten. I should also be clear that the towns themselves aren't devoid of attractions. While I highly encourage Alaska-bound cruisers to get out into the wilderness, there are plenty of worthwhile things to do in each of the main port towns. In Juneau, food tours have become popular (think: king crab bisque and Alaska salmon). The Alaska State Museum is beautiful and worth a visit. Skagway is like a gold rush-themed movie set. You should at least walk its main street (Broadway), with its wooden-board sidewalks. If you're a craft beer fan like me, you also might want to sample a Spruce Tip Blonde Ale at Skagway Brewing Company. It's made with Sitka spruce tips picked locally in the spring. In Ketchikan, you should save a few minutes to stroll up Creek Street along Ketchikan Creek, where you might spot salmon running. It's the ultimate Alaska selfie spot. How to book the best Alaska shore excursions The simplest way to book an Alaska shore excursion is through your cruise line. You check a box on an online form before sailing or while on board, and — poof! — it's all arranged. Your cruise line will send a ticket to your room, and a tour guide will be waiting for you when you walk off the ship. Another way to go is to book directly with a tour operator in one of the ports. That said, many of the tour operators you'll find in Alaskan ports are the same tour operators that operate the ship-sponsored excursions. Often, the tours that the local tour operators will sell you are the same tours that the cruise lines are selling you at the same price. Shopping around isn't necessarily going to get you anywhere. Indeed, in some cases, the cruise lines own the tour operators in Alaska ports, or, at least, a piece of them. For instance, the parent company of Princess Cruises and Holland America is a part-owner of Skagway's big attraction, the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway. Note that you can sometimes get discounts by calling a tour operator directly. I've had some luck with that over the years, but it's hit or miss. Below, I've listed six of my all-time favorite Alaska shore excursions. These all are tours that you'll find in the lineups at every major cruise line that operates in Alaska. Different lines sometimes have different names for these tours — and sometimes different pricing. For the listings below, I've used the tour names and pricing listed in the current tour sheets at Princess, which, along with sister line Holland America, is the biggest cruise operator in Alaska. Note that all of these tours are located in the three most-visited cruise ports in Alaska: Juneau, Skagway and Ketchikan. There are some great tours in lesser visited ports such as Sitka and Icy Strait Point, too, but they didn't make my Top Six list. Dogsledding and glacier adventure by helicopter For those with a hefty bankroll, this might be the ultimate Alaska shore excursion. Combining helicopter flightseeing over the seemingly endless Juneau Icefield with a landing on a glacier for dogsledding, it hits two of Alaska's most iconic experiences. It's also extremely expensive, as I know from firsthand experience. I once took my entire family of five on this excursion, dropping more than $2,000 in the process (this was back when the pricing was half what it is today — the cost goes up every year). That's a huge chunk of change for an outing that lasts just three hours. But I'll tell you this: I don't regret doing it. Not one bit. For starters, the views of the Juneau Icefield as you fly to and from the dogsledding camp are incredible (assuming the weather cooperates). But the real joy was seeing my three young girls interacting with the teams of Alaskan huskies that live at the camp. Once you arrive, you'll meet the dogs and their mushers, see where they live, get a quick tutorial in mushing and then head out for a spin around the camp on a dog-pulled sled. Note that there is a weight surcharge for participants weighing more than 250 pounds (fully clothed) for this tour, and participants must be at least 2 years old. If it's Alaska's famous humpback whales that you want to see, you'll want to book a whale-watching tour. The waters around Juneau are particularly known for humpback whales, so much so that the operator of this excursion offers a whale-sighting guarantee. Setting off from the Juneau harbor in a whale-watching boat, you'll cruise to nearby areas to see not just humpback whales but harbor seals and sea lions, too. You might even spot a killer whale or porpoise. The boat used for this excursion has both indoor and outdoor viewing areas. The trips last about four hours, including transfer time from your cruise ship to the whale-watching boat. Note that if you have a big enough group, it sometimes pays to arrange a private boat out of Juneau to take you to see humpback whales. Many lines offer a private boat charter for whale watching as a tour option, or you can arrange one through a local company. If you're like me, you may be a little terrified at the idea of climbing the sheer face of a rock cliff. But don't let that scare you away from this 3 1/4-hour tour. It's a hoot. Experienced climbing guides will meet you at your ship and drive you up the Klondike Highway to an area of granite cliffs that's the perfect playground for beginner and more seasoned climbers alike. Upon arrival, the guides provide you with all the gear you need (climbing shoes, helmets and harnesses) for a safe scramble up a 70-foot-high wall. They'll also offer plenty of instruction (and encouragement), plus a snack of trail mix and hot chocolate. If it all sounds a bit daunting, know that you don't need any experience in climbing to do it; I sure didn't have any when I tried it, nor did my young daughters, who absolutely loved it. There are multiple routes up the cliffs, some perfect for beginners. After making it to the top, you'll rappel back down — an entirely different kind of thrill. Note that children must be at least six years old to participate in this tour, and there is a weight maximum (300 pounds) and minimum (50 pounds) for participants. Call it the iconic attraction of Skagway. A ride into the mountains on this narrow-gauge railroad is the tour everybody takes when visiting the gold rush town-turned-tourist hub ... and for good reason. It offers an easy way to get deep into the great Alaskan outdoors. Truth be told, I'm a fan of more active excursions. But for someone who isn't going to hike, bike, horseback ride or raft their way through the wilderness around Skagway (there are tours for all those things, too), this nearly three-hour ride on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway is one of the best ways to get a glimpse of the area's classic Alaskan scenery. From the comfort of a vintage railcar, you'll get stunning views of mountains, gorges, glacial rivers and waterfalls as you climb nearly 3,000 feet to the summit of White Pass, the headwaters to the mighty Yukon River. Designated an International Historic Civil Engineering Landmark, the 20-mile route is a marvel in its own right, with improbably steep grades at times and segments that pass over soaring wooden trestles and around tight cliff-hugging curves. Laughton Glacier Hike and White Pass Rail Adventure This is another tour with a sky-high cost, but, in my opinion, it's well worth the money. Indeed, it's one of my all-time favorite Alaska shore excursions. The nearly 10-hour, Skagway-based outing begins with a transfer from your ship to the starting point for the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway, mentioned above, where you'll join some of your fellow passengers on a train ride deep into the mountains. But unlike your fellow passengers on the traditional White Pass Scenic Railway ride, you won't stay on board for the full 20-mile trip into the wilderness. Instead, you'll hop off about 14 miles inland, at a drop-off point called Glacier Station. From there, you'll set off on a 6- to 8-mile round-trip guided wilderness hike on a trail along the Skagway River. The highlight of the hike is a magnificent view of Laughton Glacier. Returning to Glacier Station, you'll end the day with a ride back to Skagway on the White Pass & Yukon Route Railway, which makes a special stop to pick you up. Note that the minimum age to do this tour is 9 years old, and participants should be in good shape for the long hike. In addition, you'll need to carry a passport with you or other compliant document to enter Canada, as you will be stepping onto Canadian soil while traversing part of the trail. Misty Fjords National Monument by seaplane There's nothing that says Alaska quite like a trip into the wilderness in a floatplane. And, if you're going to do a floatplane ride, there's nowhere better in Ketchikan. You'll find a small armada of floatplanes just down from the cruise ship docks waiting to take you to nearby Misty Fjords National Monument. Misty Fjords is one of those quintessential Alaska destinations that's so beautiful you just want to cry. That is, if it's not too "misty" to see it. It got its name for a reason. The area is often shrouded in clouds and drizzly rain. Ketchikan is known as one of the rainiest places in North America, with over 13 feet of rain each year. So, yeah, bring a rain jacket. But, also get ready for lovely views of glacier-carved fjords, cliffs and rock walls jutting thousands of feet out of the ocean. The whole thing is covered with temperate rainforests and features huge waterfalls (thanks to all that rain). It's definitely a sight to see. Note that there often are two versions of this tour available: one that is about two hours long and only includes flightseeing, and a slightly longer version that includes a water landing within Misty Fjord National Monument. This is also a tour that has skyrocketed in price in recent years. When I last wrote about it just a couple of years ago, it cost about $200 per person less than it does now. Planning a cruise?
